﴿And Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing﴾: this is an indication of His knowledge of the believers and of His lifting the disbelievers' hand from them, and of His knowledge of the peace with the disbelievers at Hudaybiyyah, since it was the cause of the mixing of the Arabs, the conversion of many of them, and the elevation of the word of Islam. In the year of Hudaybiyyah they numbered one thousand four hundred, and two years later they marched on Makkah with ten thousand.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: in this verse there are subtle meanings. God made clear the utmost difference between the disbeliever and the believer. He distinguished between the two agents, since the agent of *ja'ala* (made) is the disbelievers, and the agent of *anzala* (sent down) is God, the Exalted. He distinguished between the two objects: that is zealotry, and this is tranquility. He distinguished between the two annexations: He annexed zealotry to ignorance and annexed tranquility to God, the Exalted. And between the two verbs, *ja'ala* and *anzala*: zealotry is made in the present state, in an accident that does not last, while tranquility is like something kept safe in the treasury of mercy, so He sent it down. Zealotry is ugly and blameworthy in itself and became uglier by its attribution to ignorance, while tranquility is good in itself and became better by its attribution to God, the Exalted. The conjunction in *fa-anzala* with *fa* (then) rather than *wa* (and) indicates correspondence. You say: Zayd honored me, so I honored him; the *fa* indicates reciprocation through correspondence, and for this reason he made it *fa-anzala*. Since the Messenger (ﷺ) was the one who first agreed to the peace, while the believers were resolved to fight, and were determined not to return to their families until Makkah was conquered or they sacrificed at the place of sacrifice, and refused except to write "Muhammad, Messenger of God (ﷺ)" and "In the name of God," God said: *upon His Messenger*. When he (ﷺ) became tranquil for the peace, the believers became tranquil, so He said: *and upon the believers*. Since the believers were with God, the Exalted, they were obligated to that word, as He said: *Indeed, the most noble of you with God is the most pious of you* [al-Hujurat: 13]. This contains a summary, and it is a fine statement.

His Almighty and Majestic saying:

﴿Certainly Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree. He knew what was in their hearts, so He sent down tranquillity upon them and rewarded them with a near victory.﴾ ﴿And many spoils that they will take. And Allah is ever Almighty, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿Allah promised you many spoils that you will take, and He hastened this one for you, and restrained the hands of the people from you, that it might be a sign for the believers and guide you to a straight path.﴾ ﴿And another [gain] you were not able to achieve, but Allah has already encompassed it, and Allah is over all things capable.﴾ ﴿And if those who disbelieved had fought you, they would have turned their backs; then they would find neither a protector nor a helper.﴾ ﴿[This is] the way of Allah that has already passed before, and you will never find any change in the way of Allah.﴾ ﴿And it is He who restrained their hands from you and your hands from them in the valley of Makkah after He had given you victory over them. And Allah is ever Seeing of what you do.﴾ ﴿They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from al-Masjid al-Haram, and the sacrificial animals were held back from reaching their place of sacrifice. And were it not for believing men and believing women whom you did not know, that you might trample them and thereby incur blame upon you without knowledge [of them]—[it would have happened], so that Allah might admit into His mercy whom He wills. If they had been separated, We would have punished those among them who disbelieved with a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿When those who disbelieved had put into their hearts zealotry—the zealotry of the time of ignorance—then Allah sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and made them adhere to the word of piety, and they were more deserving of it and worthy of it. And Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing.﴾

When Allah, the Exalted, mentioned the state of those who stayed behind from the journey with the Messenger (ﷺ), He mentioned the state of the sincere believers who travelled with him. The verse indicates Allah's pleasure with them, and for this reason it is called the Pledge of Good Pleasure (Bay'at al-Ridwan). According to what has been narrated, they numbered one thousand five hundred and twenty. Ibn Abi Awfa said: and three hundred [more].

The origin of this pledge is that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) alighted at al-Hudaybiyah, he sent Jawwas ibn Umayyah al-Khuza'i as a messenger to the people of Makkah, and mounted him on his camel called al-Tha'lab, informing them that he had come as a pilgrim (mu'tamir) and did not intend fighting. When he came to them and spoke with them, they hamstrung his camel and wanted to kill him, but the Ahabish protected him. When this reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he intended to send Umar. He said: "You know my harshness (faẓaẓati), and they hate me, and there is no one from Banu 'Adi there who would protect me. But I will direct you to a man who is more honoured than me and more beloved to them: Uthman ibn Affan." So he sent him, and he informed them that he had not come for war, but had come only as a visitor to this House, honouring its sanctity. When Aban ibn Sa'id ibn al-'As met him, he dismounted from his mount, carried him upon it, and gave him protection. Quraysh said to him: "If you wish, circumambulate the House; but as for your entering upon us, there is no way to that." He said: "I will not circumambulate it until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) circumambulates it."

al-Hudaybiyah was ten miles from Makkah. A crier from the army shouted: "Uthman has been killed!" So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers became incensed and said: "We will not leave if this is true until we meet the people." Then the herald of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called out: "The pledge, the pledge!" Then the Holy Spirit descended, and they all pledged allegiance except al-Jadd ibn Qays, the hypocrite. Al-Sha'bi said: The first to pledge was Abu Sinan ibn Wahb al-Asadi. The governing element (al-'amil) in "when" (idh) is "was pleased." Good pleasure, according to this, means the manifestation of blessings upon them; so it is an attribute of action (sifat fi'l), not an attribute of essence (sifat dhat), since it is restricted by time. "Under" (taht) may be taken as relating to "they pledge allegiance to you," or as a circumstantial element (hal) from the object, because he (ﷺ) was sitting beneath it at its base. Abdullah ibn al-Mughaffal said: "I was standing over his head, and in my hand was a branch of the tree, which I was using to ward off [insects] from him, and I raised the branch from his back." They pledged to him to die before him and not to flee. He said to them: "You today are the best people on earth." The tree was a samura tree (a kind of acacia). Bukayr ibn al-Ash'aj said: on the day of the Conquest of Makkah. Nafi' said: people used to come to that tree and pray beside it, and this reached Umar, so he ordered it to be cut down. This pledge took place in the sixth year of the Hijrah. And a hadith from him (ﷺ) says: "No one who witnessed the Pledge of Good Pleasure will enter the Fire."

﴿He knew what was in their hearts﴾: Qatadah and Ibn Juraij said: [it was] the good pleasure with the pledge, that they would not flee. Al-Farra' said: [it was] truthfulness and fidelity. al-Tabari and Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: [it was] faith and its soundness, love for the religion and eagerness for it. It has also been said: [it was] their concern and their turning away from the polytheists, and their disdain for that, in accordance with what Umar and others expressed; and this is a good view, for it entails the descent of tranquillity and the allusion to the near victory. Tranquillity (sakinah) is the settling of their hearts and their being made submissive to accept the command of Allah, the Exalted. According to the previous views, it is said that this statement does not clearly require the sending down of tranquillity, unless it is construed as being in exchange for tranquillity, the near victory and the spoils. Muqatil said: [He knew] what was in their hearts of aversion to pledging to fight with him to the death, ﴿so He sent down tranquillity upon them﴾ until they pledged. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This contains a reproach to the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. End of quotation.

﴿And rewarded them with a near victory﴾: Qatadah and Ibn Abi Layla said: the conquest of Khaybar, which occurred directly after their return from Makkah. al-Hasan said: the conquest of Hajar, which was the greatest conquest, from whose dates they benefited for a long time. It has also been said: the conquest of Makkah; and "nearness" is a relative matter, but the conquest of Khaybar was nearer. al-Hasan and Nuh the reciter read "wa-ataahum" (and gave them), meaning "gave them," while the majority read "wa-athaba-hum" from reward (thawab).

﴿And many spoils﴾: that is, the spoils of Khaybar, which was land with estates and wealth, and he divided it among them. It has also been said: the spoils of Hajar; and it has been said: the spoils of Persia and Rome. The majority read "yaakhudhunaha" with the letter ya', in the third person, in harmony with "wa-athabahum" and the preceding third-person pronoun. al-A'mash, Talhah, Ruways from Ya'qub, Dulbah from Yunus from Warsh, Abu Dihyah, Siqlab from Nafi', and al-Antaki from Abu Ja'far read it with ta' in the second person, as came after "Allah promised you many spoils," which is in the second person. These promised spoils are those which came after this, and will continue until the Day of Resurrection, as said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and the majority of the exegetes.

The domain of Islam has greatly expanded, and the Muslims conquered countless lands and gained spoils that cannot be counted, in both east and west of the lands, even in the lands of India, and in the lands of Sudan in our own age. There came to us on pilgrimage one of the kings of Ghana from the lands of Takrur, and it was mentioned about him that he conquered more than twenty-five kingdoms of the lands of Sudan, and they embraced Islam, and he came to us with some of their kings who performed pilgrimage with him. It has been said: the address is to the people of the pledge, and that they will gain many spoils. Zayd ibn Aslam and his son said: the many spoils are the spoils of Khaybar. ﴿So He hastened this one for you﴾: the reference of "this" is to the pledge and to deliverance from the matter of Quraysh through the truce; this was said by Ibn Abbas, Zayd ibn Aslam, and his son. Mujahid said: the spoils of Khaybar.

﴿And restrained the hands of the people from you﴾: that is, the people of Makkah, through the truce. Ibn Abbas said: Uyaynah ibn Hisn al-Fazari, Awf ibn Malik al-Nadri, and those who were with them, when they came to support the people of Khaybar while the Messenger (peace be upon him) was besieging them, Allah placed terror in their hearts and restrained them from the Muslims. Ibn Abbas also said: Asad and Ghatafan were allies of Khaybar. al-Tabari said: [Allah] restrained the Jews from Madinah after the Messenger (ﷺ) went out to al-Hudaybiyah and to Khaybar.

﴿That it might be﴾: that is, this restraint might be a sign for the believers, and a token by which they know that they are in a position with Allah, the Exalted, and that He guarantees their victory and triumph over them. It has also been said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw the conquest of Makkah in his dream, and the dreams of the prophets are true; so this was delayed until the following year, and the conquest of Khaybar was made a sign and an indication of the conquest of Makkah. Thus the pronoun in "li-takuna" refers to "this," namely the spoils of Khaybar. The waw in "wa-li-takuna" is superfluous according to the Kufans, and conjunctive upon an omitted element according to others, meaning: so that they might thank Him, and that it might be [a sign]; or: He promised, and hastened, and restrained, so that it would benefit you and that it might be [a sign]; or [the clause] is delayed, or what it relates to is supposed to be delayed, meaning: the doing of that.

﴿And guide you to a straight path﴾: that is, the path of reliance (tawakkul) and committing affairs to Him. It has also been said: insight and mastery.

﴿And another [gain] you were not able to achieve﴾: Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and Muqatil said: the lands of Persia and Rome and what the Muslims conquered. al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd, and Ibn Ishaq said: Khaybar. Qatadah and al-Hasan said: Makkah; and this view is consistent with the meaning and supported by it. In His saying "you were not able to achieve," there is an indication that an attempt at it had preceded and that attaining the desired object had been missed at the time, as happened in Makkah. al-Zamakhshari said: it refers to the spoils of Hawazin in the Battle of Hunayn. He also said: "you were not able to achieve," because of the retreat that occurred in it. al-Zamakhshari allowed that "wa-ukhra" might be in the genitive case by the implied "rubba" (many a); but this is strange, because "rubba" does not occur as a preposition in the Qur'an, despite its frequent occurrence in the speech of the Arabs; so how can it be used implicitly? Rather, it appears that "wa-ukhra" is in the nominative case as the subject, since it is described by the clause after it, and "qad ahata" (Allah has encompassed) is its predicate. It may also be in the accusative case by an implied verb interpreted by the meaning of "qad ahata Allahu biha" (Allah has encompassed it): meaning, "and Allah decreed another." Al-Zamakhshari mentioned these two possibilities. The meaning of "qad ahata Allahu biha" is by power and dominance over its people, meaning that it was already foreknown in His knowledge, and it became clear that they would not be able to achieve it.

﴿And if those who disbelieved had fought you﴾: this is based on the difference of opinion regarding His saying, "And He restrained the hands of the people from you": are they the polytheists of Makkah, or the supporters of the people of Khaybar, or the Jews? ﴿They would have turned their backs﴾: that is, they would have been overcome and routed.

﴿The way of Allah﴾: is in the position of an emphatic infinitive for the content of the sentence before it, meaning: Allah established for His prophets a way (sunnah), which is His saying, "I and My messengers will surely prevail" (al-Mujadilah: 21).

﴿And it is He who restrained their hands﴾: that is, He decreed between you the mutual restraint and withholding, after He had granted you victory and dominance over them. It was narrated about the cause of it that Quraysh gathered a group of their youths and placed them with Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, and they went out seeking an opportunity against the army of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When the Muslims perceived them, the Messenger (peace be upon him) sent Khalid ibn al-Walid, whom he then named "the Sword of Allah," with a group of people, and they fled before them until they drove them into the houses of Makkah, and they captured a number of them and brought them to the Messenger (ﷺ), and he showed them favour and released them. Qatadah said: that occurred at al-Hudaybiyah near a camp, which was in the valley of Makkah. From Anas: eighty men from the people of Makkah descended upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the mountain of al-Tan'im, armed, intending to take him by surprise, so we seized them and he spared them. In the hadith of Abdullah ibn Ma'qil, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked against them, and Allah seized their sight, and he said to them: "Did you come under anyone's covenant? Did anyone grant you safe-conduct?" They said: "No, by Allah." So he let them go. Al-Zamakhshari said: he meant by this restraint the day of the Conquest, and Abu Hanifah cited it as evidence that Makkah was conquered by force (anwatan) and not by treaty (sulhan). It has also been said: that was in the Battle of al-Hudaybiyah, because it was narrated that Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl went out with five hundred men, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent someone who routed him and drove him to the walls of Makkah. From Ibn Abbas: Allah made the Muslims prevail over them with stones until they drove them into the houses. End of quotation. The majority read "bima ta'malun" in the second person; Abu 'Amr read it with ya', and it is a threat to the disbelievers.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 48, verses 18–26 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿They are the ones who disbelieved﴾: meaning the people of Makkah. Ibn Khalawayh said: It is said *al-hadyu*, *al-hidyu* and *al-hida'*, three dialects. End of quote. The majority of readers recited *al-hadyu* with a sukun on the *dal*, which is the dialect of Quraysh, and so did Ibn Hurmuz, al-Hasan, Isma (via Asim), al-Lu'lu'i, and Kharija (via Abu Amr). *Wa-al-hadiyyu* (with a kasra on the *dal* and a shaddah on the *ya'*) is also read, and the two are dialects. It is coordinated with the pronoun in *sadadukum* (they barred you). *Ma'kufan* is a circumstantial state (*hal*), meaning detained, held back. *'Akaftu al-rajula 'an hajatihi* means I held the man back from his need. Abu Ali (al-Farisi) denied that *'akafa* takes a direct object, but Ibn Sida, al-Azhari and others reported it. This detention may come from the polytheists through their barring, or from the Muslims, because of their hesitation and their deliberation over the matter. Al-Ju'fi reported from Abu Amr *wa-al-hadyi* with a genitive, coordinated with *al-Masjid al-Haram*, meaning and [they barred you] from sacrificing the offering. He also read it in the nominative, on the assumption of an implied *wa-sadda al-hadyi* (and the barring of the offering). The Prophet had set out with him one hundred camels, according to Muqatil. It was also said seventy. The people numbered seven hundred men, so one camel was for every ten, as reported by al-Miswar ibn Makhrama and Ubayy ibn al-Hakam.

﴿Until it reaches its place of sacrifice﴾: al-Shafi'i said: the Haram. Abu Hanifa used this to argue that the place of sacrifice for one who is prevented (*al-muhsar*) is the Haram, not the place where he was prevented. Al-Farra' said: wherever its slaughter is permitted. *An yablugha* may be attached to *al-sadd* (barring), meaning they barred the offering, and this would be a substitution of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*, a substitute that is included in the thing it replaces), meaning they barred the offering's reaching its place. Or it could be an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*), meaning out of aversion to its reaching its place. It may also be attached to *ma'kufan*, meaning detained for the sake of its reaching its place, making it an object of purpose, with the detention coming from the Muslims. Or it means detained from reaching its place, with the detention coming from the polytheists. There were people among the Muslims in Makkah who were mixed in with the polytheists, not distinguishable from them, and whose locations were not known. God said: *Had it not been that you might trample upon men who are believers, whom you do not know, and so guilt would befall you on their account without knowledge, [He would have allowed you to enter]* ... and so on, meaning: were it not for the dislike that you might kill believing men among the polytheists while you did not recognize them, and a hardship and harm would fall on you because of their killing, He would not have restrained your hands from them. The answer to *law la* (if not) is omitted because the context indicates it. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that *law tazayyalu* (if they had been separated) is like a repetition of *law la* (if not) with *rijalun mu'minun* (believing men), since both return to one meaning, and the answer would be *la-'adhdhabna* (We would have punished). End of quote. His statement that both return to one meaning is not correct, because what the first *law la* is connected to is not what the second is connected to. The meaning of the first is: were it not for the trampling of believing people; the meaning of the second is: if they had been distinguished from the disbelievers. This is a meaning clearly different from the first. *An tatauhum* (that you trample them) is a substitution of inclusion for *rijal* (men) and what follows it. It was also said it is a substitute for the pronoun in *ta'lamuhum* (you do not know them), meaning you did not know their trampling, that it was the trampling of believers. This is far-fetched. *Al-wat'* means to tread upon, and it is used metaphorically for destruction by the sword or otherwise. The poet said:

*You trod upon us with a trampling in rage, the trampling of one bound, firm in his old age.*

And in a hadith: "O God, tighten Your grip upon Mudar." *Lam ta'lamuhum* (you did not know them) is an adjective for *rijal* and *nisa'* (men and women), in which the masculine form predominates. The meaning is: you did not know their identities or that they were believers. Ibn Zayd said: *al-ma'arrah* means sin. Ibn Ishaq said: blood money. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is weak, because there is no sin or blood money in killing a believer whose faith is hidden among the people of war. Al-Tabari said: it is expiation (*kaffarah*). Al-Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: *al-ma'arrah* is that the disbelievers would reproach them and say: they killed the people of their own religion. It was also said: blame, and the soul would be pained by it for the rest of time. Al-Zamakhshari, following his habit of assembling his speech from the statements of others and giving the impression that these are his own questions and answers, gathered from these sayings a question and an answer. He said: *If you ask*: what harm would befall them if they killed them while they did not know? *I answer*: there would befall them the obligation of blood money and expiation, and the bad talk of the polytheists that they did to people of their own religion what they did to us without distinction, and sin if some negligence occurred on their part. End of quote.

﴿Without knowledge﴾ [Muhammad: 38]: this is information about the Companions and their noble quality of abstaining from sin and refraining from transgression, to the extent that if they had harmed anyone in that, it would have been without intention, like the statement of the ant about the army of Solomon: *while they do not perceive* [an-Naml: 18]. *Bi-ghayri 'ilm* (without knowledge) is attached to *an tatauhum* (that you trample them). It was also said it is attached to His saying *fa-tusibakum minhum ma'arrah* (guilt would befall you on their account) from those after you who would blame you. The majority read *law tazayyalu*, while Ibn Abi Ablah, Ibn Miqsam, Abu Haywa and Ibn 'Awn read *law tazayalu*, on the pattern of *tafa'alu*, so that *li-yudkhila* (that He may admit) is attached to an implied element indicated by the meaning. That is, the withholding of the domination over the people of Makkah and the withholding of the punishment was [for the purpose of admitting].

﴿That Allah may admit into His mercy whom He wills﴾: this implied element is understood from the answer to *law* (if). The meaning of *tazayyalu* is: if they had departed from Makkah, that is, if the believers had separated from the disbelievers and parted from them. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to both believers and disbelievers, meaning if some of them had separated from others.

﴿When those who disbelieved put in their hearts zealotry, the zealotry of ignorance﴾: *idh* (when) is governed by *la-'adhdhabna* (We would have punished), or by *law sadduckum* (if they had barred you), or by an implied *udhkur* (remember). *Al-hamiyyah* is the sense of honor and pride. It is said: *hamaytu 'an kadha hamiyyatan* (I was zealous about such a thing) when you feel honor and pride to refrain from something and feel shame at doing it. Al-Mutalammis said:

*Except that I am among them, and my honor is their honor, as the head protects its nose from being crushed.*

Al-Zuhri said: their zealotry is their pride in refusing to acknowledge the Messenger of God (ﷺ) as a messenger, and in opening with *bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim* (In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful). The one who refused this was Suhayl ibn 'Amr. Ibn Bahr said: their zealotry is their partisanship for their gods, and the pride is that they would worship anything other than them. It was also said: they killed our fathers and brothers, then they would enter upon us in our houses, and by al-Lat and al-'Uzza they will never enter it. This was zealotry of ignorance because it had no proof and was not in its proper place. It was merely blind partisanship, since he (ﷺ) came only to honor the House and did not intend war. They were in this like the poet who spoke of the zealotry of ignorance:

*Am I anything but of Ghazziyyah? If she goes astray, I go astray, and if Ghazziyyah is rightly guided, I am rightly guided.*

*Hamiyyata* (zealotry) is a substitute for *al-hamiyyah*. *Al-sakinah* (tranquility) is composure and calm, so they were composed and forbearing. *Kalimat al-taqwa* (the word of piety) is: *la ilaha illa Allah* (there is no god but God). This was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), and this is the view of 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, 'Amr ibn Maymun, Qatada, Mujahid, Ikrima, al-Dahhak, Salama ibn Kuhayl, Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Talha ibn Musarrif, al-Rabi', al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and Mujahid also said: it is *la ilaha illa Allah wahdahu la sharika lah, lahu al-mulk wa lahu al-hamd, wa huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadir* (there is no god but God alone, with no partner, to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs praise, and He is over all things capable). 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with both of them, said: *la ilaha illa Allah, wa Allahu akbar* (there is no god but God, and God is greatest). Abu Hurayra and 'Ata' al-Khurasani said: *la ilaha illa Allah, Muhammad rasul Allah (ﷺ)* (there is no god but God, Muhammad is the messenger of God). The word is attributed to piety because it is the cause of piety and its foundation. It was also said it is by omitting a modifier, meaning the word of the people of piety. Al-Miswar ibn Makhrama and Marwan ibn al-Hakam said: the word of piety here is *bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim* (In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful), which the disbelievers of Quraysh refused, so God obliged the believers with it and made them most worthy of it. It was also said: their saying "We hear and obey."

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in *wa-kanu* (and they were) refers to the believers, and the one being preferred over is omitted, meaning *ahqqa biha* (most worthy of it) than the disbelievers of Makkah, because God chose them for His religion and for the companionship of His Prophet (ﷺ). It was also said: than the Jews and Christians. This worthiness is in this world. It was also said: most worthy of it in God's knowledge. It was also said: *wa-ahlaha* (and its people) in the Hereafter, with reward. It was also said: the pronoun in *wa-kanu* refers to the disbelievers of Makkah, because they are the people of God's sanctuary, and among them is His Messenger, had they not been deprived of divine guidance.

﴿And Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing﴾: this is an indication of His knowledge of the believers and of His lifting the disbelievers' hand from them, and of His knowledge of the peace with the disbelievers at Hudaybiyyah, since it was the cause of the mixing of the Arabs, the conversion of many of them, and the elevation of the word of Islam. In the year of Hudaybiyyah they numbered one thousand four hundred, and two years later they marched on Makkah with ten thousand.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: in this verse there are subtle meanings. God made clear the utmost difference between the disbeliever and the believer. He distinguished between the two agents, since the agent of *ja'ala* (made) is the disbelievers, and the agent of *anzala* (sent down) is God, the Exalted. He distinguished between the two objects: that is zealotry, and this is tranquility. He distinguished between the two annexations: He annexed zealotry to ignorance and annexed tranquility to God, the Exalted. And between the two verbs, *ja'ala* and *anzala*: zealotry is made in the present state, in an accident that does not last, while tranquility is like something kept safe in the treasury of mercy, so He sent it down. Zealotry is ugly and blameworthy in itself and became uglier by its attribution to ignorance, while tranquility is good in itself and became better by its attribution to God, the Exalted. The conjunction in *fa-anzala* with *fa* (then) rather than *wa* (and) indicates correspondence. You say: Zayd honored me, so I honored him; the *fa* indicates reciprocation through correspondence, and for this reason he made it *fa-anzala*. Since the Messenger (ﷺ) was the one who first agreed to the peace, while the believers were resolved to fight, and were determined not to return to their families until Makkah was conquered or they sacrificed at the place of sacrifice, and refused except to write "Muhammad, Messenger of God (ﷺ)" and "In the name of God," God said: *upon His Messenger*. When he (ﷺ) became tranquil for the peace, the believers became tranquil, so He said: *and upon the believers*. Since the believers were with God, the Exalted, they were obligated to that word, as He said: *Indeed, the most noble of you with God is the most pious of you* [al-Hujurat: 13]. This contains a summary, and it is a fine statement.

His Almighty and Majestic saying:

﴿Certainly Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree. He knew what was in their hearts, so He sent down tranquillity upon them and rewarded them with a near victory.﴾ ﴿And many spoils that they will take. And Allah is ever Almighty, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿Allah promised you many spoils that you will take, and He hastened this one for you, and restrained the hands of the people from you, that it might be a sign for the believers and guide you to a straight path.﴾ ﴿And another [gain] you were not able to achieve, but Allah has already encompassed it, and Allah is over all things capable.﴾ ﴿And if those who disbelieved had fought you, they would have turned their backs; then they would find neither a protector nor a helper.﴾ ﴿[This is] the way of Allah that has already passed before, and you will never find any change in the way of Allah.﴾ ﴿And it is He who restrained their hands from you and your hands from them in the valley of Makkah after He had given you victory over them. And Allah is ever Seeing of what you do.﴾ ﴿They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from al-Masjid al-Haram, and the sacrificial animals were held back from reaching their place of sacrifice. And were it not for believing men and believing women whom you did not know, that you might trample them and thereby incur blame upon you without knowledge [of them]—[it would have happened], so that Allah might admit into His mercy whom He wills. If they had been separated, We would have punished those among them who disbelieved with a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿When those who disbelieved had put into their hearts zealotry—the zealotry of the time of ignorance—then Allah sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and made them adhere to the word of piety, and they were more deserving of it and worthy of it. And Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing.﴾

When Allah, the Exalted, mentioned the state of those who stayed behind from the journey with the Messenger (ﷺ), He mentioned the state of the sincere believers who travelled with him. The verse indicates Allah's pleasure with them, and for this reason it is called the Pledge of Good Pleasure (Bay'at al-Ridwan). According to what has been narrated, they numbered one thousand five hundred and twenty. Ibn Abi Awfa said: and three hundred [more].

The origin of this pledge is that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) alighted at al-Hudaybiyah, he sent Jawwas ibn Umayyah al-Khuza'i as a messenger to the people of Makkah, and mounted him on his camel called al-Tha'lab, informing them that he had come as a pilgrim (mu'tamir) and did not intend fighting. When he came to them and spoke with them, they hamstrung his camel and wanted to kill him, but the Ahabish protected him. When this reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he intended to send Umar. He said: "You know my harshness (faẓaẓati), and they hate me, and there is no one from Banu 'Adi there who would protect me. But I will direct you to a man who is more honoured than me and more beloved to them: Uthman ibn Affan." So he sent him, and he informed them that he had not come for war, but had come only as a visitor to this House, honouring its sanctity. When Aban ibn Sa'id ibn al-'As met him, he dismounted from his mount, carried him upon it, and gave him protection. Quraysh said to him: "If you wish, circumambulate the House; but as for your entering upon us, there is no way to that." He said: "I will not circumambulate it until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) circumambulates it."

al-Hudaybiyah was ten miles from Makkah. A crier from the army shouted: "Uthman has been killed!" So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers became incensed and said: "We will not leave if this is true until we meet the people." Then the herald of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called out: "The pledge, the pledge!" Then the Holy Spirit descended, and they all pledged allegiance except al-Jadd ibn Qays, the hypocrite. Al-Sha'bi said: The first to pledge was Abu Sinan ibn Wahb al-Asadi. The governing element (al-'amil) in "when" (idh) is "was pleased." Good pleasure, according to this, means the manifestation of blessings upon them; so it is an attribute of action (sifat fi'l), not an attribute of essence (sifat dhat), since it is restricted by time. "Under" (taht) may be taken as relating to "they pledge allegiance to you," or as a circumstantial element (hal) from the object, because he (ﷺ) was sitting beneath it at its base. Abdullah ibn al-Mughaffal said: "I was standing over his head, and in my hand was a branch of the tree, which I was using to ward off [insects] from him, and I raised the branch from his back." They pledged to him to die before him and not to flee. He said to them: "You today are the best people on earth." The tree was a samura tree (a kind of acacia). Bukayr ibn al-Ash'aj said: on the day of the Conquest of Makkah. Nafi' said: people used to come to that tree and pray beside it, and this reached Umar, so he ordered it to be cut down. This pledge took place in the sixth year of the Hijrah. And a hadith from him (ﷺ) says: "No one who witnessed the Pledge of Good Pleasure will enter the Fire."

﴿He knew what was in their hearts﴾: Qatadah and Ibn Juraij said: [it was] the good pleasure with the pledge, that they would not flee. Al-Farra' said: [it was] truthfulness and fidelity. al-Tabari and Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: [it was] faith and its soundness, love for the religion and eagerness for it. It has also been said: [it was] their concern and their turning away from the polytheists, and their disdain for that, in accordance with what Umar and others expressed; and this is a good view, for it entails the descent of tranquillity and the allusion to the near victory. Tranquillity (sakinah) is the settling of their hearts and their being made submissive to accept the command of Allah, the Exalted. According to the previous views, it is said that this statement does not clearly require the sending down of tranquillity, unless it is construed as being in exchange for tranquillity, the near victory and the spoils. Muqatil said: [He knew] what was in their hearts of aversion to pledging to fight with him to the death, ﴿so He sent down tranquillity upon them﴾ until they pledged. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This contains a reproach to the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. End of quotation.

﴿And rewarded them with a near victory﴾: Qatadah and Ibn Abi Layla said: the conquest of Khaybar, which occurred directly after their return from Makkah. al-Hasan said: the conquest of Hajar, which was the greatest conquest, from whose dates they benefited for a long time. It has also been said: the conquest of Makkah; and "nearness" is a relative matter, but the conquest of Khaybar was nearer. al-Hasan and Nuh the reciter read "wa-ataahum" (and gave them), meaning "gave them," while the majority read "wa-athaba-hum" from reward (thawab).

﴿And many spoils﴾: that is, the spoils of Khaybar, which was land with estates and wealth, and he divided it among them. It has also been said: the spoils of Hajar; and it has been said: the spoils of Persia and Rome. The majority read "yaakhudhunaha" with the letter ya', in the third person, in harmony with "wa-athabahum" and the preceding third-person pronoun. al-A'mash, Talhah, Ruways from Ya'qub, Dulbah from Yunus from Warsh, Abu Dihyah, Siqlab from Nafi', and al-Antaki from Abu Ja'far read it with ta' in the second person, as came after "Allah promised you many spoils," which is in the second person. These promised spoils are those which came after this, and will continue until the Day of Resurrection, as said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and the majority of the exegetes.

The domain of Islam has greatly expanded, and the Muslims conquered countless lands and gained spoils that cannot be counted, in both east and west of the lands, even in the lands of India, and in the lands of Sudan in our own age. There came to us on pilgrimage one of the kings of Ghana from the lands of Takrur, and it was mentioned about him that he conquered more than twenty-five kingdoms of the lands of Sudan, and they embraced Islam, and he came to us with some of their kings who performed pilgrimage with him. It has been said: the address is to the people of the pledge, and that they will gain many spoils. Zayd ibn Aslam and his son said: the many spoils are the spoils of Khaybar. ﴿So He hastened this one for you﴾: the reference of "this" is to the pledge and to deliverance from the matter of Quraysh through the truce; this was said by Ibn Abbas, Zayd ibn Aslam, and his son. Mujahid said: the spoils of Khaybar.

﴿And restrained the hands of the people from you﴾: that is, the people of Makkah, through the truce. Ibn Abbas said: Uyaynah ibn Hisn al-Fazari, Awf ibn Malik al-Nadri, and those who were with them, when they came to support the people of Khaybar while the Messenger (peace be upon him) was besieging them, Allah placed terror in their hearts and restrained them from the Muslims. Ibn Abbas also said: Asad and Ghatafan were allies of Khaybar. al-Tabari said: [Allah] restrained the Jews from Madinah after the Messenger (ﷺ) went out to al-Hudaybiyah and to Khaybar.

﴿That it might be﴾: that is, this restraint might be a sign for the believers, and a token by which they know that they are in a position with Allah, the Exalted, and that He guarantees their victory and triumph over them. It has also been said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw the conquest of Makkah in his dream, and the dreams of the prophets are true; so this was delayed until the following year, and the conquest of Khaybar was made a sign and an indication of the conquest of Makkah. Thus the pronoun in "li-takuna" refers to "this," namely the spoils of Khaybar. The waw in "wa-li-takuna" is superfluous according to the Kufans, and conjunctive upon an omitted element according to others, meaning: so that they might thank Him, and that it might be [a sign]; or: He promised, and hastened, and restrained, so that it would benefit you and that it might be [a sign]; or [the clause] is delayed, or what it relates to is supposed to be delayed, meaning: the doing of that.

﴿And guide you to a straight path﴾: that is, the path of reliance (tawakkul) and committing affairs to Him. It has also been said: insight and mastery.

﴿And another [gain] you were not able to achieve﴾: Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and Muqatil said: the lands of Persia and Rome and what the Muslims conquered. al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd, and Ibn Ishaq said: Khaybar. Qatadah and al-Hasan said: Makkah; and this view is consistent with the meaning and supported by it. In His saying "you were not able to achieve," there is an indication that an attempt at it had preceded and that attaining the desired object had been missed at the time, as happened in Makkah. al-Zamakhshari said: it refers to the spoils of Hawazin in the Battle of Hunayn. He also said: "you were not able to achieve," because of the retreat that occurred in it. al-Zamakhshari allowed that "wa-ukhra" might be in the genitive case by the implied "rubba" (many a); but this is strange, because "rubba" does not occur as a preposition in the Qur'an, despite its frequent occurrence in the speech of the Arabs; so how can it be used implicitly? Rather, it appears that "wa-ukhra" is in the nominative case as the subject, since it is described by the clause after it, and "qad ahata" (Allah has encompassed) is its predicate. It may also be in the accusative case by an implied verb interpreted by the meaning of "qad ahata Allahu biha" (Allah has encompassed it): meaning, "and Allah decreed another." Al-Zamakhshari mentioned these two possibilities. The meaning of "qad ahata Allahu biha" is by power and dominance over its people, meaning that it was already foreknown in His knowledge, and it became clear that they would not be able to achieve it.

﴿And if those who disbelieved had fought you﴾: this is based on the difference of opinion regarding His saying, "And He restrained the hands of the people from you": are they the polytheists of Makkah, or the supporters of the people of Khaybar, or the Jews? ﴿They would have turned their backs﴾: that is, they would have been overcome and routed.

﴿The way of Allah﴾: is in the position of an emphatic infinitive for the content of the sentence before it, meaning: Allah established for His prophets a way (sunnah), which is His saying, "I and My messengers will surely prevail" (al-Mujadilah: 21).

﴿And it is He who restrained their hands﴾: that is, He decreed between you the mutual restraint and withholding, after He had granted you victory and dominance over them. It was narrated about the cause of it that Quraysh gathered a group of their youths and placed them with Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, and they went out seeking an opportunity against the army of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When the Muslims perceived them, the Messenger (peace be upon him) sent Khalid ibn al-Walid, whom he then named "the Sword of Allah," with a group of people, and they fled before them until they drove them into the houses of Makkah, and they captured a number of them and brought them to the Messenger (ﷺ), and he showed them favour and released them. Qatadah said: that occurred at al-Hudaybiyah near a camp, which was in the valley of Makkah. From Anas: eighty men from the people of Makkah descended upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the mountain of al-Tan'im, armed, intending to take him by surprise, so we seized them and he spared them. In the hadith of Abdullah ibn Ma'qil, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked against them, and Allah seized their sight, and he said to them: "Did you come under anyone's covenant? Did anyone grant you safe-conduct?" They said: "No, by Allah." So he let them go. Al-Zamakhshari said: he meant by this restraint the day of the Conquest, and Abu Hanifah cited it as evidence that Makkah was conquered by force (anwatan) and not by treaty (sulhan). It has also been said: that was in the Battle of al-Hudaybiyah, because it was narrated that Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl went out with five hundred men, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent someone who routed him and drove him to the walls of Makkah. From Ibn Abbas: Allah made the Muslims prevail over them with stones until they drove them into the houses. End of quotation. The majority read "bima ta'malun" in the second person; Abu 'Amr read it with ya', and it is a threat to the disbelievers.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 48, verses 18–26 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿They are the ones who disbelieved﴾: meaning the people of Makkah. Ibn Khalawayh said: It is said *al-hadyu*, *al-hidyu* and *al-hida'*, three dialects. End of quote. The majority of readers recited *al-hadyu* with a sukun on the *dal*, which is the dialect of Quraysh, and so did Ibn Hurmuz, al-Hasan, Isma (via Asim), al-Lu'lu'i, and Kharija (via Abu Amr). *Wa-al-hadiyyu* (with a kasra on the *dal* and a shaddah on the *ya'*) is also read, and the two are dialects. It is coordinated with the pronoun in *sadadukum* (they barred you). *Ma'kufan* is a circumstantial state (*hal*), meaning detained, held back. *'Akaftu al-rajula 'an hajatihi* means I held the man back from his need. Abu Ali (al-Farisi) denied that *'akafa* takes a direct object, but Ibn Sida, al-Azhari and others reported it. This detention may come from the polytheists through their barring, or from the Muslims, because of their hesitation and their deliberation over the matter. Al-Ju'fi reported from Abu Amr *wa-al-hadyi* with a genitive, coordinated with *al-Masjid al-Haram*, meaning and [they barred you] from sacrificing the offering. He also read it in the nominative, on the assumption of an implied *wa-sadda al-hadyi* (and the barring of the offering). The Prophet had set out with him one hundred camels, according to Muqatil. It was also said seventy. The people numbered seven hundred men, so one camel was for every ten, as reported by al-Miswar ibn Makhrama and Ubayy ibn al-Hakam.

﴿Until it reaches its place of sacrifice﴾: al-Shafi'i said: the Haram. Abu Hanifa used this to argue that the place of sacrifice for one who is prevented (*al-muhsar*) is the Haram, not the place where he was prevented. Al-Farra' said: wherever its slaughter is permitted. *An yablugha* may be attached to *al-sadd* (barring), meaning they barred the offering, and this would be a substitution of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*, a substitute that is included in the thing it replaces), meaning they barred the offering's reaching its place. Or it could be an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*), meaning out of aversion to its reaching its place. It may also be attached to *ma'kufan*, meaning detained for the sake of its reaching its place, making it an object of purpose, with the detention coming from the Muslims. Or it means detained from reaching its place, with the detention coming from the polytheists. There were people among the Muslims in Makkah who were mixed in with the polytheists, not distinguishable from them, and whose locations were not known. God said: *Had it not been that you might trample upon men who are believers, whom you do not know, and so guilt would befall you on their account without knowledge, [He would have allowed you to enter]* ... and so on, meaning: were it not for the dislike that you might kill believing men among the polytheists while you did not recognize them, and a hardship and harm would fall on you because of their killing, He would not have restrained your hands from them. The answer to *law la* (if not) is omitted because the context indicates it. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that *law tazayyalu* (if they had been separated) is like a repetition of *law la* (if not) with *rijalun mu'minun* (believing men), since both return to one meaning, and the answer would be *la-'adhdhabna* (We would have punished). End of quote. His statement that both return to one meaning is not correct, because what the first *law la* is connected to is not what the second is connected to. The meaning of the first is: were it not for the trampling of believing people; the meaning of the second is: if they had been distinguished from the disbelievers. This is a meaning clearly different from the first. *An tatauhum* (that you trample them) is a substitution of inclusion for *rijal* (men) and what follows it. It was also said it is a substitute for the pronoun in *ta'lamuhum* (you do not know them), meaning you did not know their trampling, that it was the trampling of believers. This is far-fetched. *Al-wat'* means to tread upon, and it is used metaphorically for destruction by the sword or otherwise. The poet said:

*You trod upon us with a trampling in rage, the trampling of one bound, firm in his old age.*

And in a hadith: "O God, tighten Your grip upon Mudar." *Lam ta'lamuhum* (you did not know them) is an adjective for *rijal* and *nisa'* (men and women), in which the masculine form predominates. The meaning is: you did not know their identities or that they were believers. Ibn Zayd said: *al-ma'arrah* means sin. Ibn Ishaq said: blood money. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is weak, because there is no sin or blood money in killing a believer whose faith is hidden among the people of war. Al-Tabari said: it is expiation (*kaffarah*). Al-Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: *al-ma'arrah* is that the disbelievers would reproach them and say: they killed the people of their own religion. It was also said: blame, and the soul would be pained by it for the rest of time. Al-Zamakhshari, following his habit of assembling his speech from the statements of others and giving the impression that these are his own questions and answers, gathered from these sayings a question and an answer. He said: *If you ask*: what harm would befall them if they killed them while they did not know? *I answer*: there would befall them the obligation of blood money and expiation, and the bad talk of the polytheists that they did to people of their own religion what they did to us without distinction, and sin if some negligence occurred on their part. End of quote.

﴿Without knowledge﴾ [Muhammad: 38]: this is information about the Companions and their noble quality of abstaining from sin and refraining from transgression, to the extent that if they had harmed anyone in that, it would have been without intention, like the statement of the ant about the army of Solomon: *while they do not perceive* [an-Naml: 18]. *Bi-ghayri 'ilm* (without knowledge) is attached to *an tatauhum* (that you trample them). It was also said it is attached to His saying *fa-tusibakum minhum ma'arrah* (guilt would befall you on their account) from those after you who would blame you. The majority read *law tazayyalu*, while Ibn Abi Ablah, Ibn Miqsam, Abu Haywa and Ibn 'Awn read *law tazayalu*, on the pattern of *tafa'alu*, so that *li-yudkhila* (that He may admit) is attached to an implied element indicated by the meaning. That is, the withholding of the domination over the people of Makkah and the withholding of the punishment was [for the purpose of admitting].

﴿That Allah may admit into His mercy whom He wills﴾: this implied element is understood from the answer to *law* (if). The meaning of *tazayyalu* is: if they had departed from Makkah, that is, if the believers had separated from the disbelievers and parted from them. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to both believers and disbelievers, meaning if some of them had separated from others.

﴿When those who disbelieved put in their hearts zealotry, the zealotry of ignorance﴾: *idh* (when) is governed by *la-'adhdhabna* (We would have punished), or by *law sadduckum* (if they had barred you), or by an implied *udhkur* (remember). *Al-hamiyyah* is the sense of honor and pride. It is said: *hamaytu 'an kadha hamiyyatan* (I was zealous about such a thing) when you feel honor and pride to refrain from something and feel shame at doing it. Al-Mutalammis said:

*Except that I am among them, and my honor is their honor, as the head protects its nose from being crushed.*

Al-Zuhri said: their zealotry is their pride in refusing to acknowledge the Messenger of God (ﷺ) as a messenger, and in opening with *bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim* (In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful). The one who refused this was Suhayl ibn 'Amr. Ibn Bahr said: their zealotry is their partisanship for their gods, and the pride is that they would worship anything other than them. It was also said: they killed our fathers and brothers, then they would enter upon us in our houses, and by al-Lat and al-'Uzza they will never enter it. This was zealotry of ignorance because it had no proof and was not in its proper place. It was merely blind partisanship, since he (ﷺ) came only to honor the House and did not intend war. They were in this like the poet who spoke of the zealotry of ignorance:

*Am I anything but of Ghazziyyah? If she goes astray, I go astray, and if Ghazziyyah is rightly guided, I am rightly guided.*

*Hamiyyata* (zealotry) is a substitute for *al-hamiyyah*. *Al-sakinah* (tranquility) is composure and calm, so they were composed and forbearing. *Kalimat al-taqwa* (the word of piety) is: *la ilaha illa Allah* (there is no god but God). This was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), and this is the view of 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, 'Amr ibn Maymun, Qatada, Mujahid, Ikrima, al-Dahhak, Salama ibn Kuhayl, Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Talha ibn Musarrif, al-Rabi', al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and Mujahid also said: it is *la ilaha illa Allah wahdahu la sharika lah, lahu al-mulk wa lahu al-hamd, wa huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadir* (there is no god but God alone, with no partner, to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs praise, and He is over all things capable). 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with both of them, said: *la ilaha illa Allah, wa Allahu akbar* (there is no god but God, and God is greatest). Abu Hurayra and 'Ata' al-Khurasani said: *la ilaha illa Allah, Muhammad rasul Allah (ﷺ)* (there is no god but God, Muhammad is the messenger of God). The word is attributed to piety because it is the cause of piety and its foundation. It was also said it is by omitting a modifier, meaning the word of the people of piety. Al-Miswar ibn Makhrama and Marwan ibn al-Hakam said: the word of piety here is *bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim* (In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful), which the disbelievers of Quraysh refused, so God obliged the believers with it and made them most worthy of it. It was also said: their saying "We hear and obey."

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in *wa-kanu* (and they were) refers to the believers, and the one being preferred over is omitted, meaning *ahqqa biha* (most worthy of it) than the disbelievers of Makkah, because God chose them for His religion and for the companionship of His Prophet (ﷺ). It was also said: than the Jews and Christians. This worthiness is in this world. It was also said: most worthy of it in God's knowledge. It was also said: *wa-ahlaha* (and its people) in the Hereafter, with reward. It was also said: the pronoun in *wa-kanu* refers to the disbelievers of Makkah, because they are the people of God's sanctuary, and among them is His Messenger, had they not been deprived of divine guidance.

﴿And Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing﴾: this is an indication of His knowledge of the believers and of His lifting the disbelievers' hand from them, and of His knowledge of the peace with the disbelievers at Hudaybiyyah, since it was the cause of the mixing of the Arabs, the conversion of many of them, and the elevation of the word of Islam. In the year of Hudaybiyyah they numbered one thousand four hundred, and two years later they marched on Makkah with ten thousand.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: in this verse there are subtle meanings. God made clear the utmost difference between the disbeliever and the believer. He distinguished between the two agents, since the agent of *ja'ala* (made) is the disbelievers, and the agent of *anzala* (sent down) is God, the Exalted. He distinguished between the two objects: that is zealotry, and this is tranquility. He distinguished between the two annexations: He annexed zealotry to ignorance and annexed tranquility to God, the Exalted. And between the two verbs, *ja'ala* and *anzala*: zealotry is made in the present state, in an accident that does not last, while tranquility is like something kept safe in the treasury of mercy, so He sent it down. Zealotry is ugly and blameworthy in itself and became uglier by its attribution to ignorance, while tranquility is good in itself and became better by its attribution to God, the Exalted. The conjunction in *fa-anzala* with *fa* (then) rather than *wa* (and) indicates correspondence. You say: Zayd honored me, so I honored him; the *fa* indicates reciprocation through correspondence, and for this reason he made it *fa-anzala*. Since the Messenger (ﷺ) was the one who first agreed to the peace, while the believers were resolved to fight, and were determined not to return to their families until Makkah was conquered or they sacrificed at the place of sacrifice, and refused except to write "Muhammad, Messenger of God (ﷺ)" and "In the name of God," God said: *upon His Messenger*. When he (ﷺ) became tranquil for the peace, the believers became tranquil, so He said: *and upon the believers*. Since the believers were with God, the Exalted, they were obligated to that word, as He said: *Indeed, the most noble of you with God is the most pious of you* [al-Hujurat: 13]. This contains a summary, and it is a fine statement.

His Almighty and Majestic saying:

﴿Certainly Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree. He knew what was in their hearts, so He sent down tranquillity upon them and rewarded them with a near victory.﴾ ﴿And many spoils that they will take. And Allah is ever Almighty, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿Allah promised you many spoils that you will take, and He hastened this one for you, and restrained the hands of the people from you, that it might be a sign for the believers and guide you to a straight path.﴾ ﴿And another [gain] you were not able to achieve, but Allah has already encompassed it, and Allah is over all things capable.﴾ ﴿And if those who disbelieved had fought you, they would have turned their backs; then they would find neither a protector nor a helper.﴾ ﴿[This is] the way of Allah that has already passed before, and you will never find any change in the way of Allah.﴾ ﴿And it is He who restrained their hands from you and your hands from them in the valley of Makkah after He had given you victory over them. And Allah is ever Seeing of what you do.﴾ ﴿They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from al-Masjid al-Haram, and the sacrificial animals were held back from reaching their place of sacrifice. And were it not for believing men and believing women whom you did not know, that you might trample them and thereby incur blame upon you without knowledge [of them]—[it would have happened], so that Allah might admit into His mercy whom He wills. If they had been separated, We would have punished those among them who disbelieved with a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿When those who disbelieved had put into their hearts zealotry—the zealotry of the time of ignorance—then Allah sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and made them adhere to the word of piety, and they were more deserving of it and worthy of it. And Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing.﴾

When Allah, the Exalted, mentioned the state of those who stayed behind from the journey with the Messenger (ﷺ), He mentioned the state of the sincere believers who travelled with him. The verse indicates Allah's pleasure with them, and for this reason it is called the Pledge of Good Pleasure (Bay'at al-Ridwan). According to what has been narrated, they numbered one thousand five hundred and twenty. Ibn Abi Awfa said: and three hundred [more].

The origin of this pledge is that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) alighted at al-Hudaybiyah, he sent Jawwas ibn Umayyah al-Khuza'i as a messenger to the people of Makkah, and mounted him on his camel called al-Tha'lab, informing them that he had come as a pilgrim (mu'tamir) and did not intend fighting. When he came to them and spoke with them, they hamstrung his camel and wanted to kill him, but the Ahabish protected him. When this reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he intended to send Umar. He said: "You know my harshness (faẓaẓati), and they hate me, and there is no one from Banu 'Adi there who would protect me. But I will direct you to a man who is more honoured than me and more beloved to them: Uthman ibn Affan." So he sent him, and he informed them that he had not come for war, but had come only as a visitor to this House, honouring its sanctity. When Aban ibn Sa'id ibn al-'As met him, he dismounted from his mount, carried him upon it, and gave him protection. Quraysh said to him: "If you wish, circumambulate the House; but as for your entering upon us, there is no way to that." He said: "I will not circumambulate it until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) circumambulates it."

al-Hudaybiyah was ten miles from Makkah. A crier from the army shouted: "Uthman has been killed!" So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers became incensed and said: "We will not leave if this is true until we meet the people." Then the herald of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called out: "The pledge, the pledge!" Then the Holy Spirit descended, and they all pledged allegiance except al-Jadd ibn Qays, the hypocrite. Al-Sha'bi said: The first to pledge was Abu Sinan ibn Wahb al-Asadi. The governing element (al-'amil) in "when" (idh) is "was pleased." Good pleasure, according to this, means the manifestation of blessings upon them; so it is an attribute of action (sifat fi'l), not an attribute of essence (sifat dhat), since it is restricted by time. "Under" (taht) may be taken as relating to "they pledge allegiance to you," or as a circumstantial element (hal) from the object, because he (ﷺ) was sitting beneath it at its base. Abdullah ibn al-Mughaffal said: "I was standing over his head, and in my hand was a branch of the tree, which I was using to ward off [insects] from him, and I raised the branch from his back." They pledged to him to die before him and not to flee. He said to them: "You today are the best people on earth." The tree was a samura tree (a kind of acacia). Bukayr ibn al-Ash'aj said: on the day of the Conquest of Makkah. Nafi' said: people used to come to that tree and pray beside it, and this reached Umar, so he ordered it to be cut down. This pledge took place in the sixth year of the Hijrah. And a hadith from him (ﷺ) says: "No one who witnessed the Pledge of Good Pleasure will enter the Fire."

﴿He knew what was in their hearts﴾: Qatadah and Ibn Juraij said: [it was] the good pleasure with the pledge, that they would not flee. Al-Farra' said: [it was] truthfulness and fidelity. al-Tabari and Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: [it was] faith and its soundness, love for the religion and eagerness for it. It has also been said: [it was] their concern and their turning away from the polytheists, and their disdain for that, in accordance with what Umar and others expressed; and this is a good view, for it entails the descent of tranquillity and the allusion to the near victory. Tranquillity (sakinah) is the settling of their hearts and their being made submissive to accept the command of Allah, the Exalted. According to the previous views, it is said that this statement does not clearly require the sending down of tranquillity, unless it is construed as being in exchange for tranquillity, the near victory and the spoils. Muqatil said: [He knew] what was in their hearts of aversion to pledging to fight with him to the death, ﴿so He sent down tranquillity upon them﴾ until they pledged. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This contains a reproach to the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. End of quotation.

﴿And rewarded them with a near victory﴾: Qatadah and Ibn Abi Layla said: the conquest of Khaybar, which occurred directly after their return from Makkah. al-Hasan said: the conquest of Hajar, which was the greatest conquest, from whose dates they benefited for a long time. It has also been said: the conquest of Makkah; and "nearness" is a relative matter, but the conquest of Khaybar was nearer. al-Hasan and Nuh the reciter read "wa-ataahum" (and gave them), meaning "gave them," while the majority read "wa-athaba-hum" from reward (thawab).

﴿And many spoils﴾: that is, the spoils of Khaybar, which was land with estates and wealth, and he divided it among them. It has also been said: the spoils of Hajar; and it has been said: the spoils of Persia and Rome. The majority read "yaakhudhunaha" with the letter ya', in the third person, in harmony with "wa-athabahum" and the preceding third-person pronoun. al-A'mash, Talhah, Ruways from Ya'qub, Dulbah from Yunus from Warsh, Abu Dihyah, Siqlab from Nafi', and al-Antaki from Abu Ja'far read it with ta' in the second person, as came after "Allah promised you many spoils," which is in the second person. These promised spoils are those which came after this, and will continue until the Day of Resurrection, as said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and the majority of the exegetes.

The domain of Islam has greatly expanded, and the Muslims conquered countless lands and gained spoils that cannot be counted, in both east and west of the lands, even in the lands of India, and in the lands of Sudan in our own age. There came to us on pilgrimage one of the kings of Ghana from the lands of Takrur, and it was mentioned about him that he conquered more than twenty-five kingdoms of the lands of Sudan, and they embraced Islam, and he came to us with some of their kings who performed pilgrimage with him. It has been said: the address is to the people of the pledge, and that they will gain many spoils. Zayd ibn Aslam and his son said: the many spoils are the spoils of Khaybar. ﴿So He hastened this one for you﴾: the reference of "this" is to the pledge and to deliverance from the matter of Quraysh through the truce; this was said by Ibn Abbas, Zayd ibn Aslam, and his son. Mujahid said: the spoils of Khaybar.

﴿And restrained the hands of the people from you﴾: that is, the people of Makkah, through the truce. Ibn Abbas said: Uyaynah ibn Hisn al-Fazari, Awf ibn Malik al-Nadri, and those who were with them, when they came to support the people of Khaybar while the Messenger (peace be upon him) was besieging them, Allah placed terror in their hearts and restrained them from the Muslims. Ibn Abbas also said: Asad and Ghatafan were allies of Khaybar. al-Tabari said: [Allah] restrained the Jews from Madinah after the Messenger (ﷺ) went out to al-Hudaybiyah and to Khaybar.

﴿That it might be﴾: that is, this restraint might be a sign for the believers, and a token by which they know that they are in a position with Allah, the Exalted, and that He guarantees their victory and triumph over them. It has also been said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw the conquest of Makkah in his dream, and the dreams of the prophets are true; so this was delayed until the following year, and the conquest of Khaybar was made a sign and an indication of the conquest of Makkah. Thus the pronoun in "li-takuna" refers to "this," namely the spoils of Khaybar. The waw in "wa-li-takuna" is superfluous according to the Kufans, and conjunctive upon an omitted element according to others, meaning: so that they might thank Him, and that it might be [a sign]; or: He promised, and hastened, and restrained, so that it would benefit you and that it might be [a sign]; or [the clause] is delayed, or what it relates to is supposed to be delayed, meaning: the doing of that.

﴿And guide you to a straight path﴾: that is, the path of reliance (tawakkul) and committing affairs to Him. It has also been said: insight and mastery.

﴿And another [gain] you were not able to achieve﴾: Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and Muqatil said: the lands of Persia and Rome and what the Muslims conquered. al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd, and Ibn Ishaq said: Khaybar. Qatadah and al-Hasan said: Makkah; and this view is consistent with the meaning and supported by it. In His saying "you were not able to achieve," there is an indication that an attempt at it had preceded and that attaining the desired object had been missed at the time, as happened in Makkah. al-Zamakhshari said: it refers to the spoils of Hawazin in the Battle of Hunayn. He also said: "you were not able to achieve," because of the retreat that occurred in it. al-Zamakhshari allowed that "wa-ukhra" might be in the genitive case by the implied "rubba" (many a); but this is strange, because "rubba" does not occur as a preposition in the Qur'an, despite its frequent occurrence in the speech of the Arabs; so how can it be used implicitly? Rather, it appears that "wa-ukhra" is in the nominative case as the subject, since it is described by the clause after it, and "qad ahata" (Allah has encompassed) is its predicate. It may also be in the accusative case by an implied verb interpreted by the meaning of "qad ahata Allahu biha" (Allah has encompassed it): meaning, "and Allah decreed another." Al-Zamakhshari mentioned these two possibilities. The meaning of "qad ahata Allahu biha" is by power and dominance over its people, meaning that it was already foreknown in His knowledge, and it became clear that they would not be able to achieve it.

﴿And if those who disbelieved had fought you﴾: this is based on the difference of opinion regarding His saying, "And He restrained the hands of the people from you": are they the polytheists of Makkah, or the supporters of the people of Khaybar, or the Jews? ﴿They would have turned their backs﴾: that is, they would have been overcome and routed.

﴿The way of Allah﴾: is in the position of an emphatic infinitive for the content of the sentence before it, meaning: Allah established for His prophets a way (sunnah), which is His saying, "I and My messengers will surely prevail" (al-Mujadilah: 21).

﴿And it is He who restrained their hands﴾: that is, He decreed between you the mutual restraint and withholding, after He had granted you victory and dominance over them. It was narrated about the cause of it that Quraysh gathered a group of their youths and placed them with Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, and they went out seeking an opportunity against the army of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When the Muslims perceived them, the Messenger (peace be upon him) sent Khalid ibn al-Walid, whom he then named "the Sword of Allah," with a group of people, and they fled before them until they drove them into the houses of Makkah, and they captured a number of them and brought them to the Messenger (ﷺ), and he showed them favour and released them. Qatadah said: that occurred at al-Hudaybiyah near a camp, which was in the valley of Makkah. From Anas: eighty men from the people of Makkah descended upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the mountain of al-Tan'im, armed, intending to take him by surprise, so we seized them and he spared them. In the hadith of Abdullah ibn Ma'qil, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked against them, and Allah seized their sight, and he said to them: "Did you come under anyone's covenant? Did anyone grant you safe-conduct?" They said: "No, by Allah." So he let them go. Al-Zamakhshari said: he meant by this restraint the day of the Conquest, and Abu Hanifah cited it as evidence that Makkah was conquered by force (anwatan) and not by treaty (sulhan). It has also been said: that was in the Battle of al-Hudaybiyah, because it was narrated that Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl went out with five hundred men, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent someone who routed him and drove him to the walls of Makkah. From Ibn Abbas: Allah made the Muslims prevail over them with stones until they drove them into the houses. End of quotation. The majority read "bima ta'malun" in the second person; Abu 'Amr read it with ya', and it is a threat to the disbelievers.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 48, verses 18–26 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿They are the ones who disbelieved﴾: meaning the people of Makkah. Ibn Khalawayh said: It is said *al-hadyu*, *al-hidyu* and *al-hida'*, three dialects. End of quote. The majority of readers recited *al-hadyu* with a sukun on the *dal*, which is the dialect of Quraysh, and so did Ibn Hurmuz, al-Hasan, Isma (via Asim), al-Lu'lu'i, and Kharija (via Abu Amr). *Wa-al-hadiyyu* (with a kasra on the *dal* and a shaddah on the *ya'*) is also read, and the two are dialects. It is coordinated with the pronoun in *sadadukum* (they barred you). *Ma'kufan* is a circumstantial state (*hal*), meaning detained, held back. *'Akaftu al-rajula 'an hajatihi* means I held the man back from his need. Abu Ali (al-Farisi) denied that *'akafa* takes a direct object, but Ibn Sida, al-Azhari and others reported it. This detention may come from the polytheists through their barring, or from the Muslims, because of their hesitation and their deliberation over the matter. Al-Ju'fi reported from Abu Amr *wa-al-hadyi* with a genitive, coordinated with *al-Masjid al-Haram*, meaning and [they barred you] from sacrificing the offering. He also read it in the nominative, on the assumption of an implied *wa-sadda al-hadyi* (and the barring of the offering). The Prophet had set out with him one hundred camels, according to Muqatil. It was also said seventy. The people numbered seven hundred men, so one camel was for every ten, as reported by al-Miswar ibn Makhrama and Ubayy ibn al-Hakam.

﴿Until it reaches its place of sacrifice﴾: al-Shafi'i said: the Haram. Abu Hanifa used this to argue that the place of sacrifice for one who is prevented (*al-muhsar*) is the Haram, not the place where he was prevented. Al-Farra' said: wherever its slaughter is permitted. *An yablugha* may be attached to *al-sadd* (barring), meaning they barred the offering, and this would be a substitution of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*, a substitute that is included in the thing it replaces), meaning they barred the offering's reaching its place. Or it could be an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*), meaning out of aversion to its reaching its place. It may also be attached to *ma'kufan*, meaning detained for the sake of its reaching its place, making it an object of purpose, with the detention coming from the Muslims. Or it means detained from reaching its place, with the detention coming from the polytheists. There were people among the Muslims in Makkah who were mixed in with the polytheists, not distinguishable from them, and whose locations were not known. God said: *Had it not been that you might trample upon men who are believers, whom you do not know, and so guilt would befall you on their account without knowledge, [He would have allowed you to enter]* ... and so on, meaning: were it not for the dislike that you might kill believing men among the polytheists while you did not recognize them, and a hardship and harm would fall on you because of their killing, He would not have restrained your hands from them. The answer to *law la* (if not) is omitted because the context indicates it. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that *law tazayyalu* (if they had been separated) is like a repetition of *law la* (if not) with *rijalun mu'minun* (believing men), since both return to one meaning, and the answer would be *la-'adhdhabna* (We would have punished). End of quote. His statement that both return to one meaning is not correct, because what the first *law la* is connected to is not what the second is connected to. The meaning of the first is: were it not for the trampling of believing people; the meaning of the second is: if they had been distinguished from the disbelievers. This is a meaning clearly different from the first. *An tatauhum* (that you trample them) is a substitution of inclusion for *rijal* (men) and what follows it. It was also said it is a substitute for the pronoun in *ta'lamuhum* (you do not know them), meaning you did not know their trampling, that it was the trampling of believers. This is far-fetched. *Al-wat'* means to tread upon, and it is used metaphorically for destruction by the sword or otherwise. The poet said:

*You trod upon us with a trampling in rage, the trampling of one bound, firm in his old age.*

And in a hadith: "O God, tighten Your grip upon Mudar." *Lam ta'lamuhum* (you did not know them) is an adjective for *rijal* and *nisa'* (men and women), in which the masculine form predominates. The meaning is: you did not know their identities or that they were believers. Ibn Zayd said: *al-ma'arrah* means sin. Ibn Ishaq said: blood money. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is weak, because there is no sin or blood money in killing a believer whose faith is hidden among the people of war. Al-Tabari said: it is expiation (*kaffarah*). Al-Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: *al-ma'arrah* is that the disbelievers would reproach them and say: they killed the people of their own religion. It was also said: blame, and the soul would be pained by it for the rest of time. Al-Zamakhshari, following his habit of assembling his speech from the statements of others and giving the impression that these are his own questions and answers, gathered from these sayings a question and an answer. He said: *If you ask*: what harm would befall them if they killed them while they did not know? *I answer*: there would befall them the obligation of blood money and expiation, and the bad talk of the polytheists that they did to people of their own religion what they did to us without distinction, and sin if some negligence occurred on their part. End of quote.

﴿Without knowledge﴾ [Muhammad: 38]: this is information about the Companions and their noble quality of abstaining from sin and refraining from transgression, to the extent that if they had harmed anyone in that, it would have been without intention, like the statement of the ant about the army of Solomon: *while they do not perceive* [an-Naml: 18]. *Bi-ghayri 'ilm* (without knowledge) is attached to *an tatauhum* (that you trample them). It was also said it is attached to His saying *fa-tusibakum minhum ma'arrah* (guilt would befall you on their account) from those after you who would blame you. The majority read *law tazayyalu*, while Ibn Abi Ablah, Ibn Miqsam, Abu Haywa and Ibn 'Awn read *law tazayalu*, on the pattern of *tafa'alu*, so that *li-yudkhila* (that He may admit) is attached to an implied element indicated by the meaning. That is, the withholding of the domination over the people of Makkah and the withholding of the punishment was [for the purpose of admitting].

﴿That Allah may admit into His mercy whom He wills﴾: this implied element is understood from the answer to *law* (if). The meaning of *tazayyalu* is: if they had departed from Makkah, that is, if the believers had separated from the disbelievers and parted from them. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to both believers and disbelievers, meaning if some of them had separated from others.

﴿When those who disbelieved put in their hearts zealotry, the zealotry of ignorance﴾: *idh* (when) is governed by *la-'adhdhabna* (We would have punished), or by *law sadduckum* (if they had barred you), or by an implied *udhkur* (remember). *Al-hamiyyah* is the sense of honor and pride.
